subject: Data Footprint & Kill-Switch Scenario — processing map, subprocessors, and erasure SLAs
messages:
From: Samantha Lee <samantha@clearpathhealth.com>
To: Jasmine Liu <jasmine_liu@redwoodinference.com>
Cc: ClearPath Security Team <security@clearpathhealth.com>
Date: 2026-08-21T09:12:00-07:00
Subject: Data footprint + kill-switch scenario — initial questions

Hi Jasmine,

Thanks for taking this. We're compiling a security appendix for our board and need a short, concrete Q&A about where ClearPath data is processed when calling Redwood, which subprocessors touch any plaintext, and what happens if we hit the "kill-switch" (e.g., we terminate routing or ask for immediate erasure).

Specifics we need:
- A simple processing map (region -> hops) and the list of subprocessors per hop.
- If EU routing is enabled, under what conditions would data cross to non-EU infrastructure?
- Timeline and mechanism for on-demand erasure (both transient logs and longer audit records).
- Whether any subprocessor outside the EU sees plaintext, or if only metadata/telemetry crosses.

If you can send a short diagram and a one-page summary (we'll attach directly to our security appendix), that would be ideal. We have a short deadline — would appreciate a reply by end of week.

Best,
Samantha Lee
Senior Security PM
ClearPath Health

P.S. we may loop in legal for contractual deletion SLA language once we have the technical answers.

From: Jasmine Liu <jasmine_liu@redwoodinference.com>
To: Samantha Lee <samantha@clearpathhealth.com>
Cc: Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwoodinference.com>, Vivek Kulkarni <vivek_kulkarni@redwoodinference.com>
Date: 2026-08-21T12:45:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Data footprint + kill-switch scenario — initial questions

Samantha — thanks, and happy to help. Attaching a compact processing map and our subprocessor roster (stubs below). High-level answers up front, followed by the attachments and next steps.

Executive summary (short):
- Default execution locales: EU (eu-west-1), US (us-central-1), APAC (asia-southeast-1). For customers who opt for region pinning we honor requests to keep execution within a single region.
- Cross-border transfers: By default, requests route to the pinned region. If that region is unavailable and the customer has NOT opted out of failover, requests will failover to the nearest eligible region under strict policy and with an explanatory flag in our audit logs. Customers can opt-out; in that case requests return 503 instead of failing over.
- Subprocessors & plaintext: Only the regional compute and storage subprocessors (e.g., cloud hyperscalers providing ephemeral GPU instances) process plaintext input. We maintain encryption at-rest for caches and at-transit. Persistent backups and long-term analytics are on services we control or contractually restrict; see roster.
- Kill-switch / on-demand erase: We provide (1) an immediate routing stop (kill-switch) that revokes routing tokens and halts future requests within seconds; (2) an erase job that purges request payloads, KV caches, and ephemeral logs within 24–72 hours depending on the artifact; (3) audit-trail reduction for most customers within 30 days, with a contractual option for 7-day deletion windows for regulated customers.

Attachments (included):
- processing_map_v2.pdf — visual hop map and example failure/failover paths (EU-first, failover to US West if enabled).
- subprocessor_roster_aug2026.csv — names, role, region, contractual controls, and data access levels.
- erase_playbook.md — step-by-step actions we take for on-demand erasure and a short SLA table.

Key operational notes (non-exhaustive):
- KV cache invalidation: when kill-switch is invoked we send an immediate invalidation to all serving nodes and rotate tenant-level cache keys. That removes hot-state within seconds; full purge of persisted cache snapshots is scheduled as a high-priority job.
- Transparency: every routing change, failover, and erase job emits an immutable audit event (with customer id, timestamp, and job id). We can provide an extract for your security appendix.
- Legal/contract options: Marissa (CC'd) handles deletion SLA language if you want this baked into the contract.

If helpful, Vivek can add a short note on what the network paths look like and which subprocessors are involved when failover happens. Happy to hop on a 30m call — I included a scheduling link in the related links.

Regards,

Jasmine Liu
Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference
jasmine_liu@redwoodinference.com
Attachments: processing_map_v2.pdf (diagram), subprocessor_roster_aug2026.csv (roster), erase_playbook.md (SLA + steps)

Subject: Re: Data footprint + kill-switch scenario — a few clarifiers

Thanks Jasmine — this is useful. A couple of clarifying Qs before we include the language in our appendix: 

1) If EU is pinned and failover is allowed, does any US subprocessors ever receive the original plaintext input unredacted? Or do you redact/transform before leaving-region?
2) For the erase job: you mention 24–72 hours for ephemeral logs and 30 days for audit-trail reduction. Can you outline what falls into "ephemeral" vs "audit"? We need precise labels for our security table (e.g., request payloads, KV caches, serving logs, aggregated telemetry).
3) If we request an immediate contractual deletion at termination, is there an SLA-backed timeline for complete removal from backups and long-term analytics?

If you can drop a brief table answering the three items, that'll be perfect.

—Samantha

Subject: Re: Data footprint + kill-switch scenario — a few clarifiers

Hi Samantha — quick technical table inline to answer your three points. I'm pasting a condensed matrix here and flagging the erase_playbook sections for the formal SLA language.

1) Cross-border plaintext exposure
- Scenario: EU pinned, failover enabled -> If capacity in eu-west is exhausted and failover to us-central is triggered, the full request payload (plaintext) is routed to the serving node in us-central. We do NOT perform automatic redaction before failover because model execution requires full input.
- Controls: Customers can opt-out of failover (preferred for strict EU-only requirements). For EU-only customers we can enforce a hard-region policy (no failover) at provisioning time.

2) Artifact classification & erase window (examples)
- Request payloads (responses & prompts): ephemeral (erased on erase job) — target: 24–72 hours for purge from transient stores and caches; redundant copies scrubbed within 30 days where applicable.
- KV caches / hot-state: ephemeral — invalidation immediate, durable snapshots scrubbed within 72 hours + retained metadata for debug (pointer-only) removed within 30 days.
- Serving logs (detailed traces): short-term retention 30 days by default; we can reduce to 7 days contractually.
- Aggregated telemetry / analytics (aggregated, anonymized): retained for cost/usage analysis up to 90 days; not considered PII in normal operations but can be purged earlier under contract.

3) Contractual deletion on termination
- Baseline: standard removal timelines (above) apply and backups are rotated; final scrub from long-term backup media is scheduled within 90 days.
- SLA-backed option: We offer a paid contractual SLA for "accelerated purge": complete scrub (including long-term backups and analytics indices) within 30 days of termination with audit evidence.

Operational notes:
- Encryption & key control: customer data at-rest is encrypted with tenant-scoped keys; for Private deployments customers retain keys. Hosted customers can use our KMS integration (bring-your-key option) which gives additional assurances for backup unreadability.
- Audit evidence: erase_playbook.md contains job ids and proof artifacts we provide on request (signed timestamps, job logs with hashes).

I'll attach a short flow diagram snippet to illustrate when a plaintext hop happens and which subprocessors are involved. If you prefer, we can produce a formal appendix table for your SOC packet.

-Vivek
Director, Applied ML & Inference
